title: Optimization & Training
summary: Mathematical optimization techniques for training machine learning models, including gradient descent, regularization, and convergence strategies.
historicalContext: The backpropagation algorithm was independently discovered multiple times, first by Seppo Linnainmaa in 1970 as a general sensitivity analysis method, before being popularized for neural networks by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in 1986.

commonMisconceptions.wrong: Gradient descent will always find the optimal solution given enough time.
commonMisconceptions.correct: Gradient descent may converge to local minima, saddle points, or oscillate without converging. Learning rate, batch size, optimizer choice, and loss landscape geometry all affect convergence.

commonMisconceptions.wrong: If the loss is decreasing, the model is getting better.
commonMisconceptions.correct: Loss and accuracy are related but distinct metrics. Loss can decrease while accuracy plateaus, or loss can increase while accuracy improves (e.g., with label smoothing).

commonMisconceptions.wrong: Dropout should be active during inference to add robustness.
commonMisconceptions.correct: Dropout is disabled during inference. During training, it randomly zeros activations to prevent co-adaptation. During inference, all neurons are active.

commonMisconceptions.wrong: Batch normalization uses the current batch statistics during inference.
commonMisconceptions.correct: During inference, batch normalization uses running mean and running variance accumulated during training.
An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training dataset. A batch (or mini-batch) is a subset of data processed before updating weights.

analogies.text: Gradient descent is like hiking downhill in thick fog. You can't see the valley floor, but you can feel which direction is steeper under your feet.
analogies.limitations: Real gradient descent operates in millions of dimensions simultaneously.

analogies.text: Regularization is like a teacher who limits how many notes a student can take during a lecture. By forcing the student to be selective, the teacher ensures the student focuses on the most important concepts.
analogies.limitations: Different regularization techniques (L1, L2, dropout, data augmentation) constrain the model in fundamentally different ways.

analogies.text: Learning rate is like the volume knob on a radio. Turn it too high and the signal is distorted (overshooting). Turn it too low and you can barely hear anything (slow convergence).
analogies.limitations: Radio volume is linear and independent of content. Learning rate interacts with the loss landscape in complex ways.

curiosityFacts: Deep neural networks with millions of parameters can generalize well even when they have enough capacity to memorize random labels. This 'benign overfitting' challenges classical statistical bounds.
The classical bias-variance tradeoff is a useful framework but breaks down with modern deep learning. Double descent phenomena show that very large models can have both low bias AND low variance.
